title: Doe advanced scientific computing advisory subcommittee (ascac) report: top ten exascale research challenges
contribution: DOE ASCAC subcommittee agenda (Leyffer an acknowledged contributor, not an author) listing ten unranked exascale research challenges with findings and recommendations; its optimization part (§10.1.2) argues that once inner linear algebra is saturated the cost to reduce is the number of outer iterations, via higher-order information, concurrent-point, multifidelity and stochastic/robust methods.
problem_entry: Commissioned: DOE charge letter of 29 July 2013 asking for no more than ten technical approaches to exascale, framed by energy, memory, resilience and concurrency barriers; exascale defined as 1000x over the 2009 petascale (file pp. 7, 11-12, 86).
key_idea: Co-design ('one can't design in isolation'); for optimization, treat the sequential outer loop as the bottleneck and reduce outer iterations, with inner-loop codes exposing fidelity, resource and error information (file pp. 13, 54, 56-57, 64).
assumptions: System targets 10^18 flop/s, about 20 MW, MTBF >= 24 h, < 300 cabinets, commercial viability; optimization modelled as an outer loop evaluating one point per iteration; directions declared illustrative, not exhaustive (file pp. 56-57, 65-66).
proof_devices: n/a (no proofs); performance expression P = S x e(L,O,W) x mu(E) x alpha(R) and the SLOWER degradation checklist (file p. 67)
energy-per-operation accounting: about 12 pJ per DP flop vs about 200 pJ per instruction on a simple core (file pp. 17-18)
experiments: none (cited evidence only: NTV measurements, Tianhe-2 17.8 MW for 33.86 PFlop/s, voltage-regulator experiment; file pp. 15, 17, 19)
positioning: Builds on prior exascale reports and the DARPA study [71]; for optimization cites the Acta Numerica MINLP survey [10], Floudas [46], Horst et al. [61], Neumaier [88]; distances exascale from HPL/Linpack (file pp. 11, 27, 56, 72, 76-78).
writing: Each challenge section closes with an 'Impact' subsection; findings and recommendations stated twice; national-competitiveness advocacy; section style admitted to vary with contributing experts (file pp. 8-10, 14, 22, 57, 72-75).
limits_future: Agenda only; optimization section about 1.5 pages and illustrative; defers to the forthcoming Exascale Mathematics Working Group report and warns exascale algorithm research must not crowd out applied math (file pp. 53, 56-57).

method_links.note: Committee voice: inner-loop solvers should expose fidelity, resource-usage and error information to the optimization outer loop, and techniques should couple tightly to the forward solve; Leyffer's authorship of §10.1.2 is inferred only (he is acknowledged, [10] is his survey).
Optimization including integer decisions [10] framed as an outer loop to be carried onto exascale simulation codes: the base-and-extension move at programme level, not in his own voice.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Precision as a tunable algorithmic resource
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Committee lists 'Approximate algorithms' that tune precision to reduce energy (context only; own-voice evidence is S082).

transferable: Once the inner solve is saturated, make the number of outer iterations the cost to reduce and list concurrent-point, multifidelity and higher-order options explicitly (file pp. 56-57).
Diagnose performance with a multiplicative factor model (SLOWER) and attribute each loss to one factor before proposing a remedy (file p. 67).
Close each section of an agenda or proposal with an 'Impact' paragraph naming the failure if the work is not done (file pp. 22, 57).
coauthors: R. Lucas (chair), J. Ang, K. Bergman, S. Borkar, W. Carlson, L. Carrington, G. Chiu, R. Colwell, W. Dally, J. Dongarra, A. Geist, G. Grider, R. Haring, J. Hittinger, A. Hoisie, D. Klein, P. Kogge, R. Lethin, V. Sarkar, R. Schreiber, J. Shalf, T. Sterling, R. Stevens; Leyffer listed among acknowledged contributors (with S. Wild, R. Ross and others), file p. 2

quotes.text: What is clear is that one-off, “heroic” forward simulations on the scale of a full machine contribute little, in isolation, to scientific knowledge.
A fundamental challenge in optimization for the exascale is thus the reduction of the number of outer loop iterations

title: It's to Solve Problems: An Interview with Roger Fletcher
contribution: Leyffer's OPTIMA interview of his PhD advisor Roger Fletcher plus a curated link bibliography, recording the Dundee research practices (start from computation, look at examples, look at numbers, be a good programmer, check counterexamples, change your mind) that Leyffer explicitly recognises from his own training.
problem_entry: Career interview for the society newsletter; Leyffer's prepared short list of Fletcher's papers plus implementation-level questions (solver for SL1QP, single-precision BQPD), advice and open problems (pp. 1-5).
key_idea: Fletcher's practice as elicited: try it yourself, look at numbers ('they're trying to tell you something'), be a good programmer, re-examine your own work; the filter came from asking why good SQP steps were thrown away; Leyffer ties it to the Dundee rule 'look at examples' (pp. 2, 4).
assumptions: n/a (interview); stated values: optimization is to solve problems, problems should come from people who have them rather than test libraries (p. 5).
proof_devices: n/a (no proofs); Fletcher describes Wolfe's degeneracy method in BQPD (make near-degenerate vertices degenerate, recurse with one scalar on the stack), reported as used in MINLP codes (p. 4)
SL1QP trust-region convergence is stronger because the subproblem is always feasible (p. 3); SLP-EQP active-set identification by LPs (p. 4)
experiments: none (anecdotes: steepest descent paper tape, slow SDP solves traced to eigenvalue nonsmoothness, half-precision LP failure; pp. 2, 5)
positioning: Fletcher credits Davidon, Powell, Reeves, Lanczos, Beale and Wolfe; Leyffer adds Burer/Dong low-rank SDP, Gould's SQP-EQP and Wright's unpublished SL1QP code, and argues for getting overlooked references picked up (pp. 2-6).
writing: Short concrete questions with technical interjections by Leyffer; Fletcher's writing advice: clear slides and papers, no 30-page convergence proofs, simple notation changed mid-project if needed (pp. 2-5).
limits_future: Evidence for Leyffer is limited to his questions and interjections; open problem named: MINLP with PDE/differential-equation constraints, which Leyffer had just lectured on; test-library tension recorded (p. 5).

method_links.note: Leyffer's own recollection that 'look at examples' was a Dundee rule; Fletcher checked Dai's BB-cycling counterexample and urges changing your mind (advisor lineage).
Lineage: 'look at numbers: they're trying to tell you something'; filter born from asking why good SQP steps were thrown away.

Leyffer: 'write software and the role of software'; Fletcher: 'be a good programmer'; Leyffer's question whether SL1QP needed a specialized solver; BQPD degeneracy handling used in MINLP codes by 'people such as you'.
Leyffer agrees ('Right. Absolutely.') that test problems are often badly selected and that real industrial problems beat 500 CUTE problems, against his library-building practice (Inner Tension 1).
Weak: the MINLP-with-PDE topic Leyffer had just lectured on is the extension he was carrying in at the time (compare S112).

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Leyffer: get all the references into the papers so that people start picking these things up; interviewer-compiled link bibliography of 54 items.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Precision as a tunable algorithmic resource
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Leyffer asks why BQPD was written in single precision; Fletcher no longer would; ten months before S082.

transferable: When a method's numbers look good but the globalization rejects steps, ask why the steps are thrown away and design a safeguard that interferes less (filter origin, p. 4).
Before concluding an idea failed, rule out an implementation bug by writing or reviewing the code yourself (p. 4).
Treat near-degeneracy as true degeneracy obscured by rounding and resolve it exactly rather than by perturbation (Wolfe's method in BQPD, p. 4).
In interviews and surveys, ask implementation-level questions and attach a link list to primary sources so overlooked work gets picked up (pp. 3, 5-6).
coauthors: Interviewee Roger Fletcher; transcription Gail Pieper

quotes.text: So, I know when I was in Dundee, one of the things you always told us was to look at examples, so this is the same idea.
One thing I would say is to look at numbers: they’re trying to tell you something.

title: Mixed-integer PDE-constrained optimization
contribution: Extended abstract (ANL/MCS-P5429-1015) that names the MIPDECO class with an application catalogue and a general formulation, announces a benchmark set, and shows one source-inversion instance modelled with binary source selection as a convex MIQP solved by MINOTAUR branch-and-bound.
problem_entry: Application catalogue (remediation, oil recovery, shale gas, solar cells, oil spills, hurricanes, wind farms, gas networks) against the received view that such problems are computationally intractable; general problem (1) with PDE equality constraints and integer w (p. 1).
key_idea: Name the class (attributed to the 2013 ExaMath position paper [4]), seed a benchmark library, and prefer binary source selection over continuous locations because the latter gives nonconvex constraints (pp. 1-2).
assumptions: Infinite-dimensional in general but function spaces deliberately avoided; example discretized first with a five-point stencil, h = 1/32, S = 3 sources, giving a convex MIQP (pp. 1-2).
experiments: One instance: MINOTAUR branch-and-bound, 759 nodes, 69 s CPU on an Intel i7 core; no baseline, no rounding-heuristic result, no mesh scaling in this text (p. 2).
positioning: Seven references, all applications plus the self-cited ExaMath13 position paper [4] and Leyffer's own oil-spill MIDO paper [7]; no algorithmic predecessors cited (p. 2).
writing: Acronym coined and attributed in the first paragraph, notation conventions fixed explicitly, 'Until recently ... intractable' as motivation, formulation choice justified with 'We prefer' (pp. 1-2).
limits_future: Review of approaches and full benchmark set announced but not in this text; one 32x32 instance; no function-space analysis, no comparison (pp. 1-2).

method_links.note: Step 4: class named publicly with challenges announced and a starting benchmark set.
Benchmark set introduced with its first instance shown and solved.
Binary source selection preferred because continuous source locations give nonconvex constraints; result is a convex MIQP.
Weak: solved with the group's own MINOTAUR toolkit.

transferable: Seed a new problem class with one tiny, convex, reproducible instance (stencil, mesh size, budget, solver, node count, CPU time stated) before the hard cases (p. 2).
Model a continuous location decision as binary selection over candidate sites to keep the discretized problem a convex MIQP (p. 2).
Introduce a new class with an application catalogue, the received 'intractable' verdict, and one formulation covering all cases on page 1 (p. 1).
coauthors: Pelin Cay, Drew Kouri, Bart van Bloemen Waanders

quotes.text: Until recently, these grand challenge problems have been regarded as computationally intractable.
We prefer the use of binary variables, because an alternative formulation, which models the source location as continuous variables, results nonlinear

title: Doing Moore with Less--Leapfrogging Moore's Law with Inexactness for Supercomputing
contribution: Shows on an inexact Newton method that energy saved by single-precision SIMD arithmetic can be reinvested in double-precision iterations to improve accuracy by factors of 10^4 to 10^11 at equal energy, with an energy model and an improvement-factor lower bound for linearly and quadratically convergent hybrids.
problem_entry: End of Moore's law and energy limits; reframes the benchmark question from 'budget needed for a quality' to 'quality achievable for a fixed energy budget' and critiques Linpack's unique-solution premise (p. 1).
key_idea: Two phases, inexactness then reinvestment; inexact Newton with BI-CGSTAB and Armijo line search, line-search failure read as precision too low; meta-strategy over precision levels because most Newton work precedes the quadratic phase (pp. 2-3, 6).
assumptions: F twice continuously differentiable with a root, no nonzero-residual safeguards (filter [18] pointed to); tridiagonal matrix-free Jacobian; energy and miss rate linear in precision; precision usable while eps > 2^(-p+s) with s = 3 lg p - 7 + delta, delta = 8; linear (or quadratic) convergence model (pp. 2-3, 7-8).
proof_devices: energy-equivalence argument: baseline energy (7) equated with hybrid energy (8) bounds high-precision iterations k2 (9) (p. 7)
accuracy bound (10) decreasing in k1, capped by attainability at both precisions, giving (11) and the improvement-factor lower bound (12) (p. 7)
quadratic-convergence analogue (13) changing the bound by a modest factor (p. 8)
bound confronted with data: 5.5e6 bound vs 1e8 measured on Rosenbrock (p. 7)
experiments: Intel i7-4770, RAPL energy via the authors' etrace2, taskset pinning on all 8 logical CPUs, median of 31 runs, IFORT 16; Laplace and chained Rosenbrock at n = 100000; four scalar/SIMD x single/double variants; reinvestment gains 1e4 (Laplace), 1e11 and 1e8 (Rosenbrock); energy vs improvement-factor tables; std deviations and line-search failures reported; switching points chosen by hand (pp. 3-6).
positioning: Builds on Palem's inexact computing [2]-[4], inexact Newton [13], JFNK [14] and mixed-precision work [9]-[12]; claims the reinvestment phase as new; ties to weather and climate inexactness work (pp. 2, 8).
writing: Boxed Significance Statement, 'mini' table of contents, the paradox named in the abstract, candid hedges ('somewhat simplistic', 'not necessarily tight', 'not yet developed an algorithm'), societal outlook at the end (pp. 1-2, 4, 7-8).
limits_future: Two tridiagonal test problems, manual switching, no nonzero-residual safeguards, linear energy model and a loose bound; future: a methodology for jointly choosing interdependent quality-cost knobs, and application to weather and climate (pp. 2-4, 7-8).

method_links.note: Explicit fairness rule (equal energy to the double baseline), fair unit (RAPL energy, median of 31, std dev), failures reported as limits, bound compared with measurement, manual switching disclosed.
Home NLP toolkit (Newton globalization, forcing terms, filter pointer [18]) carried into energy-aware HPC.
Solver failure signal (line-search failure) read online as evidence about the arithmetic precision, answered by escalating precision rather than repairing the formulation.
Weak: self-written matrix-free inexact Newton with per-kernel precision control and a self-written energy tool (etrace2).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Precision as a tunable algorithmic resource
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Two-phase inexactness plus reinvestment, meta-strategy over precision levels p1 < ... < pL, energy model linear in precision.
Asks what quality a fixed energy budget buys instead of what budget a quality needs.

transferable: Equal-budget protocol: measure the baseline's cost to reach eps, then search the largest improvement factor the hybrid reaches without exceeding it; report energy, std deviation and outer/inner iteration split (pp. 3-6).
Energy-measurement hygiene: pin identical processes to every logical CPU, take the median of 31 runs, report std deviation (p. 3).
Use globalization failure (non-descent line-search direction) as the online trigger to raise inner precision or accuracy (pp. 2, 4).
Prove a simple budget-equivalence bound, then confront it with one measured case and state how loose it is (p. 7).
coauthors: Stefan M. Wild, Mike Fagan, Marc Snir, Krishna Palem, Kazutomo Yoshii, Hal Finkel

quotes.text: In our experiments, we take this failure as an indication that the precision level was too low, and switch to a higher level of precision.
We have not yet developed an algorithm to decide automatically when to switch from single precision to double precision.
